headline: Kaepung Guns Show a Signal Before an Order
deck: Seoul says photographed 122 mm systems across from Gimpo are legacy pieces displayed openly; movement, dispersal or an operational directive would change the assessment.
body: Photographs taken from an observation deck in Gimpo showed what experts said appeared to be a North Korean self-propelled howitzer in Kaepung County, across the coastal border. [E1]

Capt. Jang Do-young, a spokesman for South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff, said the North had deployed legacy artillery along coastal areas in plain view and that it was not the new system Pyongyang had recently mentioned. [E2] This is a different development from this paper's Oct. 12 report on missile launches toward the East Sea: the new evidence is a visible deployment facing the Seoul-area border.

SBS reported that the presumed 122 mm gun has a maximum range of 24 km and is a key artillery asset heavily deployed along the front line. [E3] About three self-propelled guns were visible near the riverbank. [E4]

SBS reported that soldiers sat atop one self-propelled gun, using it as a seat while its barrel moved slowly side to side and up and down. [E5] One photographed vehicle carried a slogan calling for the annihilation of U.S. forces, Yonhap reported. [E6]
Stars and Stripes reported that several self-propelled howitzers had been moved near the southern border after North Korea threatened to deploy offensive assets there. [E7]
SBS reported that artillery normally avoids exposing its location, while these guns were brought near enough to be filmed from South Korean cameras. [E8]

**The desk's reading.** The visible, south-facing deployment makes the range a live operational signal: equipment is in place where it can be seen and is described as having been moved after a threat. The stronger competing reading is that it is practical pre-positioning for imminent use. The conspicuous exposure supports the reading of a display as well as readiness.

**The next test.** By 23:00 UTC, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff or subsequent photographs can show whether North Korean units leave the guns exposed or disperse them into covered firing positions, and whether North Korea issues an operational directive. Continued exposure without a directive would favor the display reading; dispersal or a directive would favor the pre-positioning reading.
